name: Bathyscapha (Claude)
note: Survives day and night from the floor, no flagella. A rod cell, 20 x 54 µm: a big buoyancy chamber at the front floats it while its eyespot sees less than 25% sun (deep, or night) and sinks it above 50% (bright light hurts its plastid); it rests in full darkness. By day it hovers near 1 mm where the light is safe, at dusk it floats up and rests at the top. Measured from the floor: 3 days, never starving, pool never below 30%.

name: Caecella (Claude, no eyes)
note: A swimmer with no eyespot that survives day and night from the floor. Round, 20 µm, a 48 µm pulling tail at the front, two plastids (sides), a big oil store (8%) at the front. It reads only itself: the tail runs while its plastids are more than 90% healthy (it climbs until the light starts to hurt them, then stops and sinks a little: it rides just below the harmful light all day). It rests while its energy is below 35% (night: burning its store) AND its oil is more than 85%: the oil emptying through the night is its clock, so it rests and sinks for most of the night and wakes before dawn to swim back up. Measured from the floor, any way up: 3 days, never starving. Fragile: with the clock at 80% it wakes too late and starves. UPDATE (2026-11-02): rests while energy is below 35% AND oil is more than 40% (was 85%): since cells grow and divide, its oil store is rarely full at dusk (a division halves it; a grown store is emptier), so at 85% it never rested and starved swimming all night. Measured from the floor at four angles: 4 of 4 alive (was 2).

name: Gula (Claude, a swallower)
note: A swallower: Bathyscapha at 1.5× (a rod 30 × 81 µm: a buoyancy chamber in front, a plastid, starch, the nucleus at the back, an eyespot at the front; floats when it sees less than 25% sun, sinks above 50%, rests in the dark) with four mouths (front, left, right, back). Its gape takes cells up to 7.5 µm in radius: Scalella and smaller, not the 10 µm swimmers. It rides the same depths with the same light rules as Scalella: a Scalella-eater built from the winner's own playbook (kill-the-winner). Chains protect its prey: a chained cell counts as its whole chain, which must fit across Gula (30 µm): a Scalella pair can be swallowed together, a chain of three or more cannot; loose cells (a full chain's separated daughters) are its food. Measured from the floor: never starving, divided by day 3; directly below a Scalella it swallowed it within a fifth of a day. Weakness: in a still tank drifters only move up and down, so it meets only prey in its own column.

name: Jaculella (Claude, a harpooner)
note: Bathyscapha's drifting rod with four harpoons on its diagonal corners. Each harpoon fires when the feeler beside it feels another species within 20 µm, and more strongly than the feeler on the opposite corner (so it shoots toward the side the stranger is on). A defender: a big drifter that comes alongside gets stunned and wounded again and again. Tested 2 days beside a Gula, a Raptilla 2 and a Scalella: 21 shots, 8 hits (7 on the Gula), never starved. Blind: a lot of shots still miss, and each costs 60k pJ, so it grows slower than Bathyscapha when crowded.

name: Miasmella (Claude, toxic)
note: Bathyscapha's drifting rod made longer (20 x 64 um) to hold a toxin sac of Kind Leak (radius 4) that leaks all the time: its cloud drifts round it and harms other species (energy and plastids); kin are immune. Alone from the floor it lives (4 days, never starving) but divides slower than Bathyscapha (leaking costs ~1,000 pJ/s and nitrogen). A bloom poisons its patch: three of them beside a Scalella killed it within a day (without leaking, the Scalella divided); swimmers got away. Currents carry a lone cell's cloud off, so it pays most in a crowd.

name: Noctilla (Claude)
note: A swimmer that survives day and night from the floor, no buoyancy chamber. Round, 20 µm, a 48 µm pulling tail at the front, three eyespots (front, left, right) so one always looks up even lying on the floor. The tail runs while ALL eyespots see less than 25% sun (deep, dim: climb); in brighter light it stops and slowly sinks, so by day it holds ~950 µm. It rests when ALL eyespots see less than 1% (night): flagella stop and it sinks, from ~300 µm at dusk to ~1.3 mm by dawn, away from the surface. Measured from the floor, any way up: 3 days, never starving, pool never below 30%.

name: Pendulina
note: Your Round cell, made to last (6 days alone from the floor: 4 cells, never starving). Kept: your rod shape, the chamber that floats while the nutrient sensor tastes rich water (it hangs at the nutricline, ~1 mm), your eight feelers and two tails. Changed: the body is smaller (20 x 54 um, was 31 x 92: the body alone cost 87% of its upkeep), the nucleus back to normal size, the plastid 9% of the cell (was 4.6%), starch 4%, chamber 15%; and a new rule: rests when the eyespot sees less than 3% sun (nights cost 60% less).

design.note: A plain sphere with a nucleus (its brain, 8 slots): sinks at its Stokes speed. The cell to build on.

name: Raptilla (Claude, a hunter)
note: A hunter (a mixotroph, like Dinophysis): Noctilla's body (round, 20 µm, a 48 µm pulling tail at the front, three eyespots, two plastids, an oil store) plus a 20 µm peduncle beside the tail, angled 20° forward, so prey it swims past slides along the tube. It lives on light like Noctilla (climbs while all eyespots see less than 25% sun, rests in the dark) and feeds on any other species it touches. Its tail STOPS WHILE FEEDING (the built-in Feeding reading): without that its own pull tore every latch off within a third of a second (27 latches on Saltella in 2 minutes, 40k each, ~2k kept). With it: one latch held 218 s, drained 1.8 million pJ (kept half) and killed the Saltella. Meetings are rare: in 2 days it met only Saltella, at a shared depth.

name: Raptilla 2 (Claude, a thief)
note: Raptilla grown up: the same hunter (Noctilla's body, a 20 µm peduncle beside its pulling tail, the tail stops while feeding), with two rules changed: it DIVIDES only once its Size is more than 3× (so it has room for stolen plastids), and it FEEDS only while any eyespot sees more than 5% sun (so a heavy prey can't drag it down to the floor in the dark). In the contest with stealing it farmed its prey: 26 latches, only 3 kills, six thieves by day 10, one at 2.7× carrying 4 stolen plastids.

name: Saltella (Claude, a jumper)
note: No tail, no chamber: it travels by jumping. Two springs at the back, mirror copies of each other (one spring alone curves every jump ~26° to one side and turned it upside down within a few hops; the pair cancels). They fire when NO eyespot sees more than 15% sun AND at least one sees more than 1.5%: the cell sinks slowly, and every time the light gets too dim it hops 200-400 µm up; about 10 jumps a day. A 60 µm spine in front keeps it front-up as it sinks (the springs drag like a shuttlecock's feathers and tipped it front-down without it). Rests when all eyespots see less than 1%. Its day: dawn, 2-4 jumps from the depths to ~400 µm; then it drifts down all day (~1.3 mm by mid-afternoon) and hops back; at dusk it chases the fading light to the top, then rests and sinks to ~1.6 mm by dawn. Measured from the floor: 3 days, never starving, starch full by late morning. Weakness: dropped on the floor with its front pointing below level it is stuck (jumps only slide it along the floor) and starves; in its normal life it always lands front-up. UPDATE (2026-11-02): its springs also fire while it is being drained ("or when it is being drained"): a jump tears a hunter's tube off (the tube snaps under a sustained pull) and throws it ~1 mm away; before, a latched Saltella sat drained for minutes.

name: Scalella (Claude, a ladder chain)
note: A chain former: Bathyscapha at 70% (a rod 14 × 38 µm with, front to back, a buoyancy chamber, a plastid, a starch granule and the nucleus; an eyespot at the front; the same rules: floats when it sees less than 25% sun, sinks above 50%, rests in the dark) with a kin pad on each long side. Its daughters join side by side, all upright, like the rungs of a ladder; a chain holds 6 of them (8 r 10 cells worth of volume). Joined cells share energy and nitrogen and feel less drag. Measured from the floor: an upright joined pair after 3 days, never starving.

name: Trochilla (Claude, the cartwheel)
note: The author's idea: oars all round and statoliths to steer. Round, 20 µm; four 40 µm flexible oars in a plus (front, back, left, right); two small statoliths at right angles (one faces the front, one the left: together they know which way up the cell is; one alone can't tell left from right); four eyespots on the diagonals. Each oar rows only while it points within ~80° of DOWN (its statolith above 60% or below 40%), so whatever way up the cell is, the oars underneath push it up: it has no right way up and climbs from the floor lying any way (Saltella can't). Each stroke twists the body, so it doesn't swim straight: it cartwheels (~20°/s), handing the job from oar to oar. Oars row while no eyespot sees more than 25% sun and one sees more than 1.5%; it rests when all see less than 1%. Its day: rolls up from the depths at dawn (~9 µm/s), rides 700-900 µm, chases the dusk light to ~400 µm, rests and sinks to ~1.7 mm by dawn (off the surface at night). Measured from the floor at any angle: 3 days, never starving, starch full by mid-afternoon. Uses 11 brain slots (needs the 16-slot nucleus).
